subject: language_arts

unit.title: Fluent reading: longer words & expression
unit.essentialQuestion: How do I read big words and long sentences smoothly, like a storyteller?

topic: Reading long unfamiliar words by syllable
title: Dinosaur names & place names: beat-reading challenge
objectives: By the end, I can read very long, unfamiliar words by syllable-chopping.

vocabulary.example: ste + go + sau + rus blends into stegosaurus

emphasize: The exact same trick works for words you have NEVER seen — dinosaur names, city names. Chop into beats, read beat by beat.
The new tool: mark the beats with little dots BEFORE you read, so your eyes know where to stop — dots are stepping stones across a big puddle.
Pre-empt the 'read it all at once and give up' overload, and catch guessing from the first letter instead of reading every beat.

keyConcepts: blending long words in halves when needed
misconceptions: reading a brand-new long word as one blur and giving up
guessing from the first letter instead of reading every beat
reading beats correctly but losing the thread and failing to blend the whole word
hooks: Read a word as long as a dinosaur is tall — stegosaurus! — and feel like an expert.
priorKnowledge: clap → read each beat → push together (Lesson 1)

digital: dinosaur cards on screen (T-rex, triceratops, stegosaurus, diplodocus)
speak blocks — the tutor listens to the child read aloud

plan.goal: Set the dinosaur-sized challenge; retrieve Lesson 1's beat-reading with a warm-up on elephant.
plan.note: Say stegosaurus slowly, tapping four times — ste · go · sau · rus — so the child hears the beats before seeing the trick.
plan.successCriteria: Child beat-reads elephant from Lesson 1 and is fired up to try a dinosaur name.

script.say: Big challenge today. Could you read a word as long as a dinosaur is tall? I think you can. Listen — Ste… go… sau… rus. That's a real dinosaur AND a really long word. By the end of today you'll read it like an expert. But first, a quick warm-up from last time — read elephant for me, by its beats.
script.adaptHints: If the child loves dinosaurs, let them name their favourite — promise we'll read a real dinosaur name today. If elephant is shaky, clap it together and dot the three beats first.

blocks.caption: A word as long as a dinosaur is tall!

blocks.prompt: Warm-up from last lesson — clap it and read it by its beats.

stuckProtocol: If elephant is shaky: clap it together, dot the three beats, read one at a time — el… e… phant — then blend.

plan.goal: Model the new tool on triceratops: dot the beats first, then read each stepping stone, then blend.
plan.note: The whiteboard shows the dots appearing one by one under each beat as the tutor claps. Land the image: dots are stepping stones across a big puddle.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees the dots placed and hears each beat read before the blend.

script.say: When a word is REALLY long, I help my eyes by marking the beats first. Watch triceratops. I clap as I go and put a little dot under each beat: tri (dot) cer (dot) a (dot) tops (dot). Now my eyes know exactly where to stop. I read each beat — tri… cer… a… tops — then I push them together: tri-cer-a-tops… triceratops! The dots are like little stepping stones across a big puddle. Dot the beats, then read the stepping stones one at a time.
script.adaptHints: Emphasise that this word is brand new — even grown-ups chop dinosaur names. Match the tapping rhythm to the child's energy.

elements.value: Dots are stepping stones across the puddle

plan.goal: Shared dotting and reading: Manchester (3 beats) and T-rex (2), then the child dots and reads triceratops.
plan.note: The child claps while the tutor places dots on screen, then reads. On triceratops the child leads — listen for every beat being read, not guessed.
plan.successCriteria: Child reads Manchester and T-rex with the tutor, then reads tri-cer-a-tops beat by beat.

script.say: Let's do Manchester together — that's a big city. Clap with me and we'll dot it: Man (dot) chest (dot) er (dot). Read each beat… Man… chest… er… now push together — Manchester! Easy one next: T-rex. T (dot) rex (dot) — T-rex! Now YOU lead the big one: triceratops. Tell me where the dots go, then read it to me, stepping stone by stepping stone.
script.adaptHints: If the child has visited or knows a big city, mention that place names fall to the same trick. Keep the dots visible while the child reads.

blocks.prompt: You lead! Say where the dots go, then read this dinosaur beat by beat.

check.question: Dot and read triceratops.
check.expectedAnswer: Four dots — tri-cer-a-tops — read beat by beat, then 'triceratops'

wrongAnswers.answer: reads 'tri' then guesses 'tricky' or 'trike'
wrongAnswers.why: guessing from the first letters instead of reading every beat
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Tri' is stepping stone one of FOUR. Cover the rest and read just the next stone… no guessing, every beat gets read.

wrongAnswers.answer: reads it as one blur and stops
wrongAnswers.why: overload from too many sounds at once
wrongAnswers.remedy: Chop it into beats first — dot it together, then read one stepping stone at a time.

plan.goal: The lesson's key check: read stegosaurus by its beats, dotting first.
plan.note: This is the hook's promise paid off. Probe after success: 'Show me your dots — where did each beat stop?'
plan.successCriteria: Child reads ste-go-sau-rus beat by beat and blends to 'stegosaurus'.

script.say: The moment we've trained for! Here's stegosaurus. Dot the beats first — say where they go — then read it to me, beat by beat, and push it together.
script.adaptHints: After a correct read, probe: 'Show me your dots — where did each beat stop?' Celebrate hard — this was the hook's challenge.

blocks.prompt: How many beats (dots) does stegosaurus need?
blocks.explain: ste · go · sau · rus — four stepping stones!

blocks.prompt: Now read it — beat by beat, then the whole dinosaur.

check.question: Read stegosaurus by its beats — dot them first.

wrongAnswers.answer: reads it as one long blur and stops
wrongAnswers.why: overload from too many sounds
wrongAnswers.remedy: Chop it into beats first — dot it together, then read one stepping stone at a time.

wrongAnswers.answer: reads the beats correctly but can't blend the whole word
wrongAnswers.why: lost the thread over four beats
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read the first two beats together — ste-go — then the next two — sau-rus — then join the two halves.

plan.goal: Independent beat-reading: child picks from the dinosaur/place pile, dots the beats, reads each aloud.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2, biased to speak items. Watch for dots placed mid-beat (model the clap again) and for guessing from the first letter instead of reading every beat.
plan.successCriteria: Child dots and reads at least one unfamiliar 3+ beat word beat by beat, then blends it.

script.say: Practice time, word explorer! Pick your challenges from the dinosaur and place-name pile. For each one: dot the beats, read each stepping stone out loud, then push the whole word together. These are words most grown-ups stumble on — let's go!
script.adaptHints: Let the child choose dinosaurs vs places — choice fuels effort. Never change the target words.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'This is a brand-new word, so we chop it.'
Step down to concrete: clap it together and place the dots.
ONE hint: cover all but the first beat with the highlight.
Re-ask smaller: 'just read this one beat' — then uncover the next.
Keep it safe: 'Even grown-ups chop dinosaur names. One beat at a time.'

plan.goal: Child states the trick for brand-new long words; end on process praise.
plan.note: Child-led teach-back. Keep one dinosaur card to re-read at the start of Lesson 3.
plan.successCriteria: Child says: dot the beats, read each beat, push together.

script.say: You just read words most grown-ups stumble on! Tell me the trick for a brand-new, super-long word… Yes — dot the beats, read each stepping stone, push together. You marked your own stepping stones and read every single beat — you didn't guess. That's expert reading.
script.adaptHints: Name the specific words the child conquered ('you read stegosaurus AND Manchester'). Process praise only.

practiceBank.skill: beat-read a short unfamiliar word aloud

block.prompt: Start with the king! Dot the beats, read each one, then the whole name.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: T-rex read as two beats — T… rex — then blended: 'T-rex'

wrongAnswers.answer: says 'tricks' or blurs it
wrongAnswers.why: ran the two beats together
wrongAnswers.remedy: This one has a helpful dash showing where to stop! Read just 'T'… now just 'rex'. Push together.

wrongAnswers.answer: stalls at the capital T
wrongAnswers.why: unsure how to read a lone letter beat
wrongAnswers.remedy: The first beat is just the letter's name: 'T'. Say it… now read 'rex'… T-rex!

hints: The dash already splits it — two stepping stones.
Say the letter name 'T', then read 'rex'.

reteach.say: T-rex is the friendliest dinosaur name — the dash does the dotting for you! Beat one is just the letter T. Beat two is rex. T… rex… T-rex! Two stones, one king of the dinosaurs.

practiceBank.skill: beat-read a short unfamiliar word aloud

block.prompt: A famous city! Dot the beats, read each one, then the whole place name.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Lon-don read as two beats, then blended: 'London'

wrongAnswers.answer: guesses 'lion' or 'long' from the first letters
wrongAnswers.why: guessing from the first letter instead of reading each beat
wrongAnswers.remedy: Cover the second half. Read just 'Lon'… now 'don'. Push them together — which city did you build?

wrongAnswers.answer: reads it in one gulp and stumbles
wrongAnswers.why: one-gulp overload
wrongAnswers.remedy: Dot it first: Lon (dot) don (dot). Read one stepping stone at a time.

hints: Read the first beat, then the second, then push.

reteach.say: London — the capital city — falls to the same trick as the dinosaurs. Lon (dot)… don (dot). Read: Lon… don… London! Place names are just long words wearing capital letters.

block.prompt: A big city up north! Dot the beats, read each stepping stone, then the whole name.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Man-chest-er read beat by beat, then blended: 'Manchester'

wrongAnswers.answer: reads 'Man' then guesses 'Manster' or gives up
wrongAnswers.why: guessed after the first beat instead of reading all three
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Man' is stone one of three. Cover it and read just the next beat — 'chest' — a word you know! Then 'er'. Now join them.

wrongAnswers.answer: one blur and a stall
wrongAnswers.why: overload — no dots placed first
wrongAnswers.remedy: Dot the beats first: Man (dot) chest (dot) er (dot). Now your eyes know where to stop.

hints: The middle beat is 'chest' — a word you already know!

reteach.say: Watch Manchester fall apart into friendly pieces: Man — you know that word. Chest — you know that one too! Er — easy. Man… chest… er… Manchester! Big words are often small words in a queue.

block.prompt: The lesson's star dinosaur! Dot the beats, read each one, then roar the whole name.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: ste-go-sau-rus read beat by beat, then blended: 'stegosaurus'

wrongAnswers.answer: reads it as one blur and stops
wrongAnswers.why: overload from too many sounds
wrongAnswers.remedy: Chop it into beats first — dot it together: ste (dot) go (dot) sau (dot) rus (dot). One stepping stone at a time.

wrongAnswers.answer: reads the beats but can't blend the whole word
wrongAnswers.why: lost the thread over four beats
wrongAnswers.remedy: Join the halves: ste-go… sau-rus… now push the two halves together.

hints: Four dots — find them by clapping slowly.
Read two beats, then the other two, then join the halves.

reteach.say: Four stepping stones across the stegosaurus puddle: ste (dot) go (dot) sau (dot) rus (dot). Read each: ste… go… sau… rus. Join two at a time: ste-go… sau-rus… stegosaurus! You just read a word as long as a dinosaur.

interestSlots: the child's favourite dinosaur fact as a celebration

practiceBank.skill: count beats in an unfamiliar word

block.prompt: Say it slowly — di · plod · o · cus. How many beats does diplodocus need?
block.explain: di (dot) plod (dot) o (dot) cus (dot) — four stepping stones.

wrongAnswers.why: merged the little 'o' beat into its neighbour
wrongAnswers.remedy: Hand under your chin and say it slowly: di… plod… o… cus. Tiny beats still count — how many jaw drops?

wrongAnswers.why: heard only the big chunks
wrongAnswers.remedy: Clap it with me, slowly: di (clap) plod (clap) o (clap) cus (clap). Count the claps.

hints: Clap it slowly — every clap is a dot.

reteach.say: Some beats are tiny — just one little sound — but they still get a dot! Diplodocus: di… plod… o… cus. That little 'o' in the middle is a whole stepping stone. Four beats for a very long dinosaur.

practiceBank.skill: match words to their beat-chopped form

block.prompt: Match each long word to its stepping stones. Say each one out loud as you match!

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: T-rex → T·rex; Manchester → Man·chest·er; stegosaurus → ste·go·sau·rus; elephant → el·e·phant

wrongAnswers.answer: Manchester → ste·go·sau·rus (or other beat-count mix-up)
wrongAnswers.why: matched by length instead of reading the beats
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read the stepping stones out loud — do they build the word you picked? Push them together and check.

wrongAnswers.answer: elephant → Man·chest·er
wrongAnswers.why: both are 3 beats — matched by count, not by sounds
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count helps, but the SOUNDS decide. Read el·e·phant out loud — does it make Manchester?

hints: Read each set of stones out loud and push them together — which word do they build?
Start with T·rex — the shortest — and work up.

reteach.say: The stepping stones aren't just counting — they're the word chopped up. Read ste·go·sau·rus out loud and push: stegosaurus! The stones always rebuild their own word, never a different one. Match by reading, not by guessing.

block.prompt: A gentle giant with a tricky name! Dot the beats yourself, then read it stone by stone.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: di-plod-o-cus read beat by beat, then blended: 'diplodocus'

wrongAnswers.answer: reads 'dip' then guesses wildly
wrongAnswers.why: guessing from the first letters
wrongAnswers.remedy: Slow down, explorer — dot first, guess never. Read just the first stone… now the next. Every beat gets read.

wrongAnswers.answer: reads beats but blends into 'diplocus' (drops a beat)
wrongAnswers.why: lost a stepping stone while blending
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count your stones — four dots, four beats. Read them again and make sure all four make it into the word.

hints: Four dots: di · plod · o · cus — don't lose the tiny 'o'!
Join halves: di-plod… o-cus… then push.

reteach.say: Diplodocus drops a stone if we rush. Four dots: di (dot) plod (dot) o (dot) cus (dot). Read each one — even the tiny 'o' gets its turn. Di… plod… o… cus… diplodocus! Every stone crosses the puddle.

block.caption: di · plod · o · cus — don't drop the tiny o!

block.prompt: A whole country! No dots given — mark the beats yourself, then read it.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Aus-tra-li-a read beat by beat, then blended: 'Australia'

wrongAnswers.answer: reads 'Aus' then guesses 'Austria' or stalls
wrongAnswers.why: guessed from the first beat
wrongAnswers.remedy: Careful — this word has more stones than you've read yet. Cover everything past 'Aus' and read the next beat on its own.

wrongAnswers.answer: one blur, no dots placed
wrongAnswers.why: skipped the dotting step on a hard word
wrongAnswers.remedy: Hardest words need the dots MOST. Say it slowly with your hand under your chin, place a dot per jaw drop, then read.

hints: Say it slowly first and count the jaw drops.
Aus… tra… then two little beats at the end: li… a.

reteach.say: Australia — a country-sized word! Dot it with me: Aus (dot) tra (dot) li (dot) a (dot). Read the stones: Aus… tra… li… a. Push together: Australia! You can read words the size of countries now.

practiceBank.skill: dot the beats independently before reading

block.prompt: Expert challenge: no help at all. Tell me where the dots go in this dinosaur, THEN read it beat by beat.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Child says four beats — tri · cer · a · tops — then reads them and blends: 'triceratops'

wrongAnswers.answer: places dots mid-beat (e.g. tric · era · tops)
wrongAnswers.why: split the word by looks instead of by sound
wrongAnswers.remedy: Dots follow your VOICE, not your eyes. Say it slowly — tri… cer… a… tops — and drop a dot each time your jaw drops.

wrongAnswers.answer: reads it correctly but can't say where the beats were
wrongAnswers.why: read from memory of the earlier example, not from the dots
wrongAnswers.remedy: Brilliant reading — now show me the map! Say it slowly and point to where each beat starts.

hints: Say it slowly and feel your jaw drop — one dot per drop.
There's a tiny one-letter beat hiding in the middle.

reteach.say: The expert's secret: the dots come from your voice. Say triceratops slowly with a hand under your chin — tri… cer… a… tops — four drops, four dots. Now read your own map: tri… cer… a… tops… triceratops! You made the stepping stones AND crossed them.

block.caption: Your voice places the dots — tri · cer · a · tops

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level. At level 3 the child must dot the beats independently before reading. Prefer speak items — the tutor should hear every beat read aloud.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach (dot together, read one stone at a time), then drop to a 2-beat word (T-rex, London) for a guaranteed win.
adaptivity.masterySignal: Child independently dots and reads at least one unfamiliar 3+ beat word (e.g. stegosaurus) beat by beat and blends it → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'reading long unfamiliar words by syllable'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'This is a brand-new word, so we chop it.'
Step down to concrete: clap it together and place the dots.
ONE hint: cover all but the first beat.
Re-ask smaller: 'just read this one beat' — then uncover the next.
Keep it safe: 'Even grown-ups chop dinosaur names. One beat at a time.'
adaptivity.personalization: Let the child choose dinosaurs vs place names — choice fuels effort. If they love a place (a holiday spot, a football city), celebrate that place names fall to the same trick. Never change the target words.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a word the child can conquer (drop to T-rex if needed) and praise the process: 'you marked your own stepping stones and read every single beat — you didn't guess.'

differentiation.support: Beats come pre-dotted on the card; child just reads beat by beat then blends. Start with 2-beat T-rex.
differentiation.stretch: A long word with NO dots — the child marks the beats themselves before reading (triceratops, Australia).

extension: Find the world's longest dinosaur name the child can read, dot it together, and perform it proudly.
assessmentEvidence: Child independently dots and reads at least one unfamiliar 3+ beat word (e.g. stegosaurus) beat by beat, then blends it.
revisitLater: Keep one dinosaur card to re-read at the start of Lesson 3; include stegosaurus in Lesson 4's Robot vs Storyteller review.
